newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's Bhutto fears Feb 3 vote will be rigged.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's Bhutto fears Feb 3 vote will be rigged.

text.p: Pakistan's ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto said on Tuesday that President Farooq Leghari had planned to rig the February 3 elections to stop her party from winning a parliamentary majority.

"We know the president wants the elections rigged, we know there are a number of seats that have been marked out for rigging," she told Reuters in an interview at Naudero during her campaign in her southern home province of Sindh.
Leghari dismissed Bhutto's three-year-old government on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule, dissolved the National Assembly (lower house) and set fresh elections for February 3.
Faced with a petition from Bhutto, Pakistan's Supreme Court is expected to give a ruling on Wednesday either to reinstate her government or to uphold Leghari's action.
Bhutto said she had information that the president planned to rig elections at selected polling stations and manipulate the results against her Pakistan People's Party (PPP).
"If the elections are held free and fair, the People's Party will sweep the polls," she said.
"We know special officials have been put in, we know the chief minister of Sindh has provided a list of all those presiding officers who are members of his party in select polling stations.
"The president would not want free and fair elections. But right now there seem to be cracks within his own team... It is an open question whether elections would be held free and fair or not."
Bhutto said Leghari wanted to use his handpicked caretaker government and local administration to rig the elections, but added people would reject the results if the vote was unfair.
A Pakistani monthly journal, Newsline, issued an opinion poll on Monday based on interviews in 13 cities, saying Bhutto was trailing well behind her main rival, Nawaz Sharif.

Bhutto said the PPP would fare better in rural areas because the urban elite did not need it. "The underprivileged, the downtrodden, the deprived and the discriminated are the ones who need PPP. Those with electricity, gas, telephones, schools don't need it."

Bhutto comes from a big landowning family from Sindh while her main rival Nawaz Sharif is an industrialist, but she said it was wrong to say that the elections were a contest between a feudal and an industrialist politician.

"I don't have thousands of people working for me, while industrialists do have thousands of labourers in factories," she said. "Industrialists have some degree of hold in urban areas because they have captive employees whom they could theaten, coerce and punish."
She said feudal landlords did have a vote bank under their control in the past, "but now land holdings have broken up and there is no such thing as fedualism."

Benazir denied allegations by the caretaker government and by her opponents that her administration had run the economy into trouble, saying that, despite the odds, she had cut the budget deficit and increased exports and the development budget.
She said the caretaker cabinet was undoing her achievements.
